newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - London wants to bridge the Thames with garden.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - London wants to bridge the Thames with garden.

text.p: More than 100 years after the last bridge was built across the Thames, London is alive with plans for crossings over Britain's river of liquid history.
The Thames is already straddled by 19 road and railway bridges from Kew in the west to Tower Bridge -- a gaudy Victorian drawbridge built in 1894 -- in the east.

But planners are not thinking of just another traffic crossing. They want to revive the idea of a "living bridge", including shops, apartments and hotels, last seen in London in the 18th century when Old London Bridge was destroyed.

"There are cases where great new projects of lasting value and grand scale should be built that significantly improve the quality of life in our cities. An inhabited bridge must be one such case," says Environment Minister John Gummer.

Ever-growing tourism has persuaded the authorities to consider more crossings to link the north bank, studded with historic attractions like the Houses of Parliament and St Paul's Cathedral, and the rejuvenated south bank.

Once largely derelict and ignored by Londoners, the south bank has become a cultural centre in its own right thanks to the building of a thatched-roof replica of William Shakespeare's Globe Theatre and the plan to turn the vast Bankside power station into a new Tate Gallery of Modern Art.
Tourist numbers are at record levels -- about 25 million visited Britain in 1996 -- and officials want visitors to move around without being engulfed in traffic fumes.
CONSTRASTING PLANS
One plan is for dual pedestrian bridges alongside an existing rail crossing to Charing Cross station. Another is to provide a walkway linking St Paul's to the Globe theatre.

Described as "an elegant razor-sharp blade, a minimalist intervention" by its designer, Sir Norman Foster, this bridge will have a central span of 240 metres (785 feet), possibly the longest for any pedestrian bridge in the world. A third project is far from minimalist and likely to stoke great opposition if it goes ahead -- a huge "Garden Bridge" with hedges, tropical trees, restaurants overshadowed by a two 35-storey towers containing greenhouses, hotels and apartments.
It was the popular winner of a competition organised as the centrepiece of an exhibition, Living Bridges, at London's Royal Academy, a surprise hit with Londoners late last year.

Winning French architect Antoine Grumbach believes crowns on the top of the towers -- as high as the Big Ben clock tower just a few hundred metres (yards) down the river -- will evoke flight towards the new millennium.

How to celebrate the millennium in style is a major preoccupation of Britain's Conservative government which yearns to mark London's current status as the "coolest city on the planet" with a building to rival Paris' Beaubourg Centre.

There are plans for a Millennium Dome and exhibition downriver in Greenwich. But if built, the Garden Bridge would have the biggest effect on visitors' impressions of London. Gummer believes the bridge would "complete" London as a capital city. "Such a bridge should be a destination in its own right...a civic place on the River Thames drawing people from both banks like the Charles Bridge in Prague, the Ponte Vecchio in Florence or the Ponte di Rialto in Venice."
LIVING BRIDGES A RARITY
Living bridges were popular in earlier centuries in England, northern Italy and France but, despite more than 100 projects in the past 100 years, they remain a rarity.

Old London Bridge was one of the most famous inhabited bridges, lasting about 600 years before it was demolished in 1823. It carried houses and a chapel, was ravaged by fire three times and was used to display the heads of traitors.

Despite official approval and media fascination with the project, the proposed Garden Bridge has a long way to go, in terms of financing and planning approval, before it is in a position to rival Old London Bridge.
Its glass and steel towers would contrast strongly with neighbouring buildings on the north bank of the Thames around the ancient Temple legal district.

Traditionalists also complain it would block one of the great views of London from Waterloo bridge, up the river to the Houses of Parliament and beyond, and down the river to St Paul's and the City of London financial centre.
But supporters say tradition, the basis of much of London's appeal, should take a back seat and Londoners should take a leap of faith.

"Success will depend upon turning convention on its head. Instead of starting with the physical and the financial and hoping that activity will follow, one should start with activity, for it is upon this that all else rests," the organisers of the "Living Bridge" competition said.
